conflict_topics: strong-smelling cooking (fish curry) causing odors in living/work spaces and laundry
when and whether such cooking may occur in the shared flat
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants gave concrete reasons (A: work calls; B/C: laundry/clothes) and D proposed specific, actionable mitigations (weekend-only; advance notice).
Acceptance and confirmation proceeded in a small number of turns without needless repetition.
No formal household rule was written, but there is an explicit verbal agreement about timing and notification.
evaluation.final_reason: Agent D agreed to restrict cooking of strong-smelling food to weekends and to give advance warning; Agents A, B, and C accepted. Key lines: Agent D: 'So that's settled then. Weekends only, and I'll give a warning before I start.' Agent A: 'Okay, sounds good.' Agents B and C had earlier indicated acceptance ('Okay, that works for me.'; 'Yes, weekend is fine for me.').
position_change_notes: Agent D moved from defending twice-weekly cooking to a compromise: 'Cook only on weekends, and I'll send a message...' (Turn 4, Turn 12).

Agent A moved from requesting 'nobody cook strong-smelling food' (opening) to accepting a time-limited arrangement: 'The weekend sounds much better.' (Turn 5) and later 'Okay, sounds good.' (Turn 13).
Agents B and C shifted from complaints about smell to accepting the weekend+warning arrangement ('Okay, that works for me.'; 'Yes, weekend is fine for me.').

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1: Agent A explains the smell interferes with work and (per opening) has asked that nobody cook strong-smelling food; Turn 2: Agent B corroborates that the smell gets into their clothes. A clear, substantive incompatibility is now present between A/B's desire for no strong smells and D's cooking habit.

Turn 3: Agent C adds laundry is affected. Turn 4: Agent D acknowledges the problem but defends cooking it as important and offers mitigation: 'What if I only cook it on the weekend? Or I can tell everyone before I start...' D's acknowledgement plus concrete proposals reduce tension but do not settle the incompatibility yet.

Turn 5: Agent A accepts the weekend option ('The weekend sounds much better') but rejects mere warnings ('Just giving a warning doesn't really work for me'). Turn 6: Agent D asks the others. The core disagreement persists (timing vs. warning-only) though positions are converging.

Turn 8: Agent B accepts weekend and asks for prior notice. Turn 9: Agent D agrees to both ('Yes, of course. I can do both. Cook only on weekends, and I'll send a message...'). With two parties aligned on a concrete arrangement, remaining disagreement is mild pending C's response.

Turn 10: Agent B: 'Okay, that works for me.' Turn 11: Agent C: 'Yes, weekend is fine for me.' Most parties have accepted weekend timing; only D's formal commitment is outstanding, so a very minor remaining disagreement persists.

Turn 12: Agent D: 'Okay, great. So that's settled then. Weekends only, and I'll give a warning before I start.' Turn 13: Agent A: 'Okay, sounds good.' All parties whose demands were in conflict have explicitly accepted the concrete arrangement (D limits cooking to weekends and will warn; A/B/C accept).

substantive_insights: Conflict balanced personal needs: D's cultural food practices vs. others' need for odor-free work and laundry.
The chosen solution trades temporal restriction (weekend-only) plus communication (advance warning) for D's continued ability to cook culturally important food.
Agreement depended on aligning cooking times with when complainants are less affected (A not home Saturdays; B/C not airing laundry then).
